title: The Afternoon Brief: Courts block Trump moves; Disney sues FCC over licenses
dek: Federal courts blocked the Trump administration's plan to move FBI headquarters from Maryland to Washington and declined Trump's final appeal in a Carroll defamation case. Disney and ABC sued the FCC, alleging regulatory retaliation over broadcast content.
author: GoCheckMyNews
key_fact: Three separate legal fronts constrain the Trump administration: a judge halted the FBI relocation reversal, the Supreme Court closed Trump's path to overturn a $5 million Carroll verdict, and Disney brought a First Amendment challenge to what it calls an unprecedented early license renewal order.
bottom_line: Three separate legal systems constrained Trump administration action today: a federal judge halted the FBI headquarters reversal on statutory grounds, the Supreme Court closed Trump's final appeal in a Carroll defamation case, and Disney brought a First Amendment challenge to the FCC's early license renewal order. The common thread is judicial review testing whether executive and regulatory action stays within legal bounds. Watch for the Trump administration's response to the Maryland ruling, whether it appeals or seeks congressional action; the federal judge's decision on Disney's request for a temporary restraining order in the broadcast licensing dispute; and developments in the federal investigation into Alaska's same-named Senate candidate.
body: The day's legal conflicts center on whether courts will constrain executive and regulatory power or defer to administration priorities. A federal judge blocked the Trump administration from moving FBI headquarters to the Ronald Reagan Building in Washington, finding the decision exceeded statutory authority and was arbitrary and capricious. U.S. District Judge Theodore D. Chuang, an appointee of President Barack Obama, determined that Congress had previously limited the FBI's site selection to three specific locations, and the Reagan Building was not among them. The ruling preserves the Greenbelt, Maryland site selected during the Biden administration and prevents the administration from repurposing funds allocated to the Maryland project.

In a separate matter, the Supreme Court declined to reconsider its June rejection of Donald Trump's appeal challenging a $5 million jury verdict in an E. Jean Carroll defamation case. The Court did not explain its action and there were no noted dissents. Rehearing requests are almost never granted by the Court; no such request has been approved since the 1960s, according to reporting. Trump has already paid the judgment plus interest, with Carroll's representatives confirming receipt in July. A separate $83.3 million verdict in another Carroll case remains under review at the Court.

The most significant new legal challenge came when The Walt Disney Company and ABC filed suit in federal court on August 18, 2026, challenging an order from the Federal Communications Commission that they characterize as government retaliation for the network's editorial decisions. The suit seeks to block what Disney describes as an "existential threat": an unprecedented directive requiring eight Disney-owned ABC television stations to file broadcast license renewal applications years ahead of schedule, with only thirty days to prepare filings that ordinarily take months. The licenses were not due for renewal until 2028 at the earliest. In response, the FCC disputes the retaliation claim, citing ongoing investigations into Disney's diversity practices and "The View" program's compliance with public interest standards. Disney's legal team includes prominent attorneys Beth Wilkinson and Paul Clement. The case hinges on whether the timing and content of the early renewal order, combined with documented criticism from the White House, constitute retaliation under the First Amendment, or whether the FCC's independent inquiry into Disney's public interest obligations and alleged illegal discrimination is legally sufficient ground.

On the electoral front, primary voting in Florida and Alaska narrowed general election fields. Rep. Byron Donalds won the Republican primary in Florida's gubernatorial race, while former Rep. David Jolly won the Democratic primary, setting up a November matchup to succeed term-limited Gov. Ron DeSantis. Donalds has been backed by President Trump and is a prominent member of the House Freedom Caucus. In Alaska, Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan and Democrat Mary Peltola both advanced from the state's primary to the November general election. The Alaska race carries an additional layer of complication: a federal grand jury issued subpoenas last week to compel information from witnesses related to the candidacy of Dan J. Sullivan, a former teacher running as a Republican, amid an investigation into whether his candidacy is part of a conspiracy to confuse voters. Alaska's ranked-choice voting system means that if Dan J. Sullivan advances to the top four, he could reshape the general election dynamics.
